title: Animal Behavior, Ecology, and Conservation B.S. + Zoo Biology minor
type: Animal behavior, welfare, and zoo biology
scale: Small private university · Buffalo, New York
overview: Canisius combines rigorous animal-behavior science with conservation, welfare, and ethical questions about human relationships with animals. ABEC majors may add the 18-credit Zoo Biology minor, whose curriculum includes Zoo Animal Management plus options such as Zoo Animal Husbandry, Animal Welfare, Animal Enrichment, Observational Research Methods, and zoo/aquarium internships.
fundamental: A behavior-centered B.S. that can be paired with a structured Zoo Biology minor for added husbandry, welfare, enrichment, and managed-animal preparation.
scienceFoundation: Biological principles, organismal biology, ecology, and evolution
Animal behavior theory and behavioral research methods
Quantitative and qualitative research methods
Scientific reading, writing, analysis, and presentation
Conservation science and the relationships between animals and environments
animalContent: Animal behavior, learning, cognition, and observational research methods
Animal welfare, enrichment, and applied behavior
Zoo Animal Management plus Zoo Biology minor options in husbandry and exhibitry
Wildlife conservation and human effects on animals
Zoo/aquarium, animal-behavior, conservation, and other internship pathways
experience: ABEC offers credit-bearing internships in animal-related settings. The Zoo Biology minor specifically includes zoo/aquarium internship options, and its coursework can add Zoo Animal Management, husbandry, welfare, enrichment, exhibitry, and observational methods to the behavior-centered major.
research: Students may join faculty research teams studying captive wildlife, companion animals, conservation, and the human–animal bond. The university describes opportunities to use quantitative and qualitative methods and to develop work into presentations or peer-reviewed publications.
progression: Year 1: build biology and liberal-arts foundations while sampling animal behavior, ecology, conservation, and welfare questions.
Year 2: add core behavior and ecology study, statistics or research methods, and early observation or volunteer experience.
Year 3: pursue advanced behavior/conservation electives, join a faculty project, and complete a substantial internship in a setting of interest.
Year 4: develop an independent or team research product, present the work, and use advanced electives to clarify a graduate-school or employment direction.
resume: B.S. in Animal Behavior, Ecology, and Conservation; behavioral observation and research methods; ecology and conservation; welfare and ethics; faculty research; presentation or publication potential; animal-focused internship experience.
advantages: Animal behavior and welfare are central rather than incidental electives.
The Zoo Biology minor creates a clearly defined managed-animal pathway without requiring a separate zoo-science major.
Internship and research options let students test behavior, zoo, welfare, conservation, and other animal settings before narrowing further.
tradeoffs: Zoo Biology is an 18-credit minor, not a standalone major, so students need to plan its courses around the ABEC requirements.
Many ABEC and Zoo Biology electives are not offered every semester; the university advises students to plan the minor with an advisor.
Students wanting veterinary-technology credentialing or a clinical nursing curriculum need a different professional program.
bestWhen: Especially relevant for a student who wants animal behavior to remain central while also exploring welfare, conservation, rehabilitation, training, and the human responsibilities that accompany animal work.

title: Zoo and Conservation Science B.S. · Comparative Animal Behavior
overview: Drake's Zoo and Conservation Science degree brings together biology, psychology, environmental science, and professional experience. The Comparative Animal Behavior concentration examines behavior through molecular, biological, comparative, and ecological lenses. The degree is connected to animal-care and conservation organizations in the Des Moines area, including Blank Park Zoo and the Ape Cognition and Conservation Initiative.
fundamental: An interdisciplinary zoo and conservation degree with a dedicated comparative-animal-behavior concentration and access to professional and research experiences.
scienceFoundation: Biology across molecular, organismal, and ecological scales
Psychology, learning, cognition, and comparative behavior
Environmental science and conservation
Research design, evidence analysis, and scientific communication
Animal health and disease concepts relevant to managed populations
animalContent: Comparative analysis of animal behavior
Biological and molecular determinants of behavior
Ecological factors that shape behavior
Zoo animal care, conservation, and professional practice
Cognition and behavior research with nonhuman animals
experience: The program emphasizes direct experience caring for animals and leading public education. Local connections with Blank Park Zoo, the Ape Cognition and Conservation Initiative, and other organizations create possibilities for exposure to zoo operations, animal care, cognition, and conservation.
research: The Comparative Animal Behavior curriculum teaches students to develop and carry out research and to apply behavioral methods with wild and captive populations. Projects can connect biology and psychology and may address cognition, zoo populations, ecology, or conservation questions.
progression: Year 1: begin biology, psychology, and environmental-science foundations and explore zoo and conservation work locally.
Year 2: add organismal science, statistics or methods, and core comparative-behavior coursework; seek early professional exposure.
Year 3: deepen the Comparative Animal Behavior concentration and pursue an internship or sustained experience in animal care, research, education, rehabilitation, or conservation.
Year 4: complete advanced research and concentration work, producing a strong writing, analysis, or presentation sample.
resume: B.S. in Zoo and Conservation Science with Comparative Animal Behavior concentration; interdisciplinary biology and psychology; conservation; research design; professional experience connecting behavior questions to zoo and conservation practice.
advantages: A named comparative-behavior concentration provides more depth than a general zoo-science curriculum alone.
The program emphasizes both direct professional experience and the ability to develop and execute research.
The program connects zoo practice with behavior, cognition, ecology, and conservation rather than treating keeper work as its only outcome.
tradeoffs: The major is relatively new, so its long-term graduate outcomes are less established than those of older programs.
Students should examine the exact science prerequisites needed for veterinary school or highly specialized graduate programs.
A zoo-focused degree may be less flexible than broad biology for a student who later moves entirely away from animal or conservation work.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when zoo or conservation work is appealing but the strongest intellectual interest is in why animals behave as they do, including learning and cognition.

title: Zoo & Conservation Science B.S.
overview: Otterbein's Zoo & Conservation Science program combines biological science with unusually structured experiences at the Columbus Zoo and Aquarium, Ohio Wildlife Center, and the university's equine facility. Students encounter zoo research, wildlife rehabilitation, veterinary techniques, enrichment, welfare assessment, training, husbandry, conservation, and animal-focused upper-level biology.
fundamental: A science-based, highly experiential degree that moves among zoo animal care, wildlife rehabilitation, welfare, behavior, conservation, and undergraduate research.
scienceFoundation: Biology, chemistry, mathematics, and statistics appropriate to the B.S. route
Animal nutrition, reproduction, anatomy, and organismal biology
Conservation biology, aquatic biology, and ecology
Research design, observation, data collection, and scientific communication
Animal health and welfare concepts

Wildlife rehabilitation and hands-on veterinary techniques
Enrichment design, welfare assessment, and animal training
Animal nutrition, reproduction, vertebrate and invertebrate biology
Zoo, wildlife, aquarium, and conservation research topics
experience: The sequence begins with a first-year zoo research project, continues with sophomore practica at Ohio Wildlife Center, and adds junior practica at the Columbus Zoo and Otterbein's equine facility. Internships can emphasize animal care, research, operations, education, or conservation at partner and external sites.
research: A senior can pursue undergraduate research in animal behavior, visitor studies, conservation, primates, birds, amphibians and reptiles, coral-reef ecology, freshwater systems, or wildlife-rehabilitation records. Research is tied to both faculty interests and professional partners.
progression: Year 1: complete foundational science and the introductory zoo course with an observational research project at the Columbus Zoo.
Year 2: continue core biology and work through wildlife-rehabilitation practica at Ohio Wildlife Center.
Year 3: complete zoo/equine practica involving welfare, enrichment, training, and behind-the-scenes work; prepare for or complete an internship.
Year 4: select advanced animal and conservation biology and complete a focused undergraduate research project.
resume: B.S. in Zoo & Conservation Science; repeated partner-based practica; wildlife rehabilitation and animal-health exposure; zoo observation and husbandry; enrichment, welfare, and training; internship; senior research.
advantages: Experiential learning is sequenced across several years rather than left entirely to optional internships.
Students see zoo care, wildlife rehabilitation, research, education, welfare, and conservation as connected forms of work.
The Columbus Zoo and Ohio Wildlife Center partnerships provide concrete professional settings for coursework.
tradeoffs: Admission to the Zoo track occurs after enrollment and capacity is limited; applicants should verify the current selection process and contingency options.
The degree is specialized and may offer less room than broad biology for unrelated electives or a second major.
Hands-on access does not make zoo employment automatic; internships, references, and a strong record remain important in a competitive field.
bestWhen: Especially relevant for a student who wants repeated, structured contact with zoo and rehabilitation settings while still building a biological-science and research foundation.

title: Animal Behavior B.S.
overview: Bucknell's Animal Behavior major deliberately connects biology and psychology. The B.S. includes core biology, chemistry, statistics, quantitative study, learning, biopsychology, animal behavior, advanced research methods, and upper-level choices such as behavioral ecology, neuroethology, physiology, cognition, primatology, mammalogy, conservation genetics, and wildlife disease.
fundamental: A research-centered animal-behavior degree integrating biological, psychological, ecological, evolutionary, physiological, and quantitative approaches.
scienceFoundation: Core biology and chemistry
Learning, biopsychology, and behavioral science
Statistics and additional quantitative study
Advanced experimental, laboratory, or field research methods
Scientific literature, journal-style writing, and conference-style presentation

Behavioral ecology and evolution
Neuroethology, physiology, endocrinology, and neurophysiology
Comparative cognition, primatology, and primate minds
Organismal electives such as mammalogy, ornithology, amphibian biology, and invertebrate zoology
experience: The required advanced methods course has students develop hypotheses, conduct experimental research, analyze evidence, present conference-style results, and write a journal-style paper. Additional laboratory, field, and independent-research experience depends on selected electives and faculty opportunities.
research: Research methods and a senior culminating seminar are built into the major. The curriculum supports mechanistic, cognitive, ecological, evolutionary, and organismal approaches, making it possible to develop a focused research identity before graduate school.
progression: Year 1: begin animal behavior, biology, and statistics while exploring whether cognition, ecology, physiology, or evolution is most compelling.
Year 2: complete the biology sequence, learning, biopsychology, chemistry, and additional quantitative work.
Year 3: take advanced methods and upper-level animal-behavior electives; join a faculty lab or pursue independent research.
Year 4: deepen a specialty through advanced electives and complete the senior seminar with substantial literature, writing, and presentation work.
resume: B.S. in Animal Behavior; integrated biology and psychology; statistics and quantitative study; experimental or field methods; journal-style research writing; conference-style presentation; advanced study in a selected behavior specialty.
advantages: The program gives equal intellectual weight to biological mechanisms and psychological approaches to behavior.
Research design, analysis, writing, and presentation are explicit required outcomes.
A wide upper-level menu lets students explore cognition, physiology, ecology, evolution, or particular animal groups.
tradeoffs: The major is more research-oriented than vocational; husbandry, rehabilitation, zoo operations, and animal-care credentials require outside experience.
A small private residential university has a very different cost and campus profile from the regional public options.
Students pursuing direct animal-care employment need to build substantial hands-on hours alongside the academic program.
bestWhen: Especially relevant for a student drawn to animal behavior as a scientific question and considering research or graduate study in cognition, learning, neuroethology, behavioral ecology, or comparative biology.

title: Animal Studies B.A.
scale: Small private liberal-arts college · St. Petersburg, Florida
overview: Eckerd's Animal Studies major examines animals and human–animal relationships through natural science, social science, and the humanities. It includes behavior, research methods, statistics, ethics and culture, and a required practicum. Faculty and collaborative projects span cognition, welfare, communication, behavior, training, conservation, human perceptions, and the roles of animal-serving organizations.
fundamental: A broad interdisciplinary degree for studying animals and their relationships with people through scientific, social, cultural, ethical, and applied perspectives.
scienceFoundation: Animal behavior and life-history concepts
Statistics and quantitative research skills
Qualitative, critical, and interdisciplinary research methods
Scientific and humanistic analysis of human–animal relationships
Communication, writing, and ethical reasoning
animalContent: Animal behavior, cognition, communication, and training
Animal welfare and the role of zoos, aquariums, shelters, and sanctuaries
Animal-assisted interventions
Human attitudes, cultures, policies, and practices involving animals
Conservation, rehabilitation, husbandry, advocacy, and education contexts
experience: The required Practicum in Animal Studies involves at least 130 hours with an approved animal-related organization plus structured reflection. Recent and listed settings include zoos, aquariums, sanctuaries, shelters, guide-dog organizations, rehabilitation programs, and government or research facilities.
research: The Animal Studies Research Collaborative connects multiple laboratories and research groups. Projects described by the college include canine creativity, elephant cooperation, dolphin and parrot cognition, orangutan space use, animal welfare, communication, and human–animal relationships.
progression: Year 1: explore the interdisciplinary foundations of animal studies and begin biology, psychology, statistics, or humanities support courses.
Year 2: take animal behavior and research-oriented coursework while sampling welfare, cognition, conservation, culture, or assisted-intervention topics.
Year 3: join a research group or independent project and complete the 130-hour practicum in a carefully selected setting.
Year 4: use advanced electives and the capstone to integrate evidence from multiple disciplines around a specific animal-related question.
resume: B.A. in Animal Studies; animal behavior and human–animal studies; statistics; quantitative and qualitative research; a 130-hour practicum; interdisciplinary writing and communication; optional cognition, welfare, sanctuary, zoo, or conservation research.
advantages: The program treats animal work as biological, behavioral, ethical, cultural, and organizational rather than only as natural science.
A required practicum gives every major a substantial real-world experience.
Research and local placement options include cognition, welfare, zoo/aquarium, sanctuary, shelter, rehabilitation, and human-services settings.
tradeoffs: As a B.A. with an interdisciplinary focus, it does not automatically provide the same chemistry, physics, and advanced biology depth as a zoology or biology B.S.
Students targeting veterinary, physiology, or laboratory-intensive graduate programs may need a second major, minor, or carefully planned science prerequisites.
The breadth is valuable for exploration but requires deliberate choices to create a clear specialty and technical portfolio.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when the student is interested not only in animal behavior, but also in welfare, ethics, animal-serving organizations, communication, and the many ways people and animals affect one another.

title: Wildlife Care and Rehabilitation B.S.
scale: Small environmental university · in-person at Pineland, Maine
overview: Unity's in-person Wildlife Care and Rehabilitation program is an applied pathway focused on wildlife care techniques, rehabilitation strategies, animal behavior, anatomy, and habitat design. It is more directly vocational than a broad zoology or ecology degree and is designed around immersive classes and career preparation for work involving injured, orphaned, displaced, or managed wildlife.
fundamental: An applied, in-person degree centered on the practical science and decision-making involved in wildlife care, rehabilitation, behavior, anatomy, and habitat design.
scienceFoundation: Animal anatomy and physiology
Animal behavior and welfare
Wildlife biology and ecological context
Health, care, rehabilitation, and release-related decision-making
Habitat and enclosure design
animalContent: Wildlife-care techniques and rehabilitation strategies
Species-appropriate husbandry, nutrition, and behavior
Preventing habituation and supporting release readiness
Animal handling, health observation, and care records
Habitat design and the relationship between care and natural behavior
experience: The program is presented as immersive and in person, with applied learning in wildlife-care techniques and rehabilitation practice. Prospective students should ask exactly which experiences involve live animals, which occur in simulations or laboratories, and which depend on external placements.
research: This is primarily an applied professional pathway rather than a conventional research-intensive wildlife biology degree. Students considering research graduate programs should examine available statistics, research design, independent study, and faculty-project opportunities.
progression: Year 1: build biology, anatomy, and animal-behavior foundations and learn safe, ethical approaches to wildlife care.
Year 2: develop husbandry, nutrition, health-observation, habitat, and rehabilitation-planning skills.
Year 3: apply the science in increasingly complex case-based or field experiences and seek a substantial placement with a rehabilitation or wildlife-care organization.
Year 4: complete advanced applied work and assemble evidence of handling, records, care planning, communication, and professional judgment.
resume: B.S. in Wildlife Care and Rehabilitation; applied wildlife-care and husbandry concepts; animal behavior and anatomy; rehabilitation planning; habitat design; health observation; documented experiential learning.
advantages: The degree directly names and teaches wildlife care and rehabilitation rather than requiring students to assemble the topic from unrelated electives.
Its applied emphasis may help a student test the day-to-day realities of care work earlier.
Behavior, anatomy, care, and habitat are treated as connected parts of rehabilitation.
tradeoffs: The program is narrower than zoology, biology, or wildlife ecology and may be less flexible if interests shift toward laboratory science or ecosystem management.
Wildlife rehabilitation employment can be limited and experience-dependent; the degree alone does not replace permits, supervised hours, or role-specific credentials.
The current Unity model includes several distinct in-person and online pathways, so applicants should verify the exact degree length, delivery format, campus, and experiential commitments.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when the student wants to understand the practical realities of caring for wild animals and is comfortable choosing a more specialized applied degree.

title: Animal and Veterinary Sciences B.S.
overview: UMaine's Animal and Veterinary Sciences degree builds a foundation in animal biology, nutrition, disease, physiology, management, and related sciences. Students can shape the degree toward animal science, equine study, pre-veterinary preparation, or pre-veterinary microbiology. Hands-on work at the J. Franklin Witter Teaching and Research Center emphasizes dairy cattle and standardbred horses.
fundamental: A biologically rigorous, hands-on animal-science degree centered on health, physiology, nutrition, disease, reproduction, and management of domestic animals, with strong pre-veterinary relevance.

Animal anatomy and physiology
Nutrition, genetics, reproduction, and disease
Animal management and agricultural systems
Pre-veterinary science requirements where selected
animalContent: Dairy cattle and equine care and management
Animal health, disease, nutrition, and reproduction
Domestic-animal handling and husbandry
Veterinary and biomedical preparation
Animal research and production systems
experience: Hands-on domestic-animal experience is a central requirement. At the Witter Teaching and Research Center, students work with dairy cattle and standardbred horses and can build competence toward increasingly responsible management tasks.
research: The Witter Center supports teaching and research in animal science and sustainable agriculture, and UMaine's research-university environment creates additional laboratory and faculty-project options. The most visible program focus is domestic-animal health, management, and agricultural research.
progression: Year 1: begin biology and chemistry while gaining early exposure to domestic-animal care and management.
Year 2: add anatomy, physiology, nutrition, genetics, or microbiology and increase practical responsibility at the teaching farm.
Year 3: follow the selected concentration, pursue faculty research or a veterinary/animal-industry internship, and complete advanced animal-science work.
Year 4: finish advanced health, reproduction, management, or pre-veterinary requirements and produce a research, internship, or professional portfolio.
resume: B.S. in Animal and Veterinary Sciences; substantial biological and laboratory science; animal anatomy, physiology, nutrition, disease, reproduction, and management; hands-on dairy and equine experience; concentration-specific veterinary or research preparation.
advantages: Strong preparation in animal health, physiology, nutrition, reproduction, and management.
Students gain repeated hands-on responsibility with live domestic animals rather than only occasional exposure.
The public research-university setting supports pre-veterinary prerequisites and faculty research opportunities.
tradeoffs: The program's practical core is centered on dairy cattle, horses, agriculture, and pre-veterinary science—not wildlife, zoo animals, or comparative behavior.
A student focused on wild-animal behavior, field ecology, or conservation would find a more direct route in UMaine Wildlife Ecology or Zoology.
Behavior, cognition, enrichment, and wildlife rehabilitation would need to be developed through electives and external experience.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when animal health, veterinary preparation, physiology, nutrition, or hands-on domestic-animal management is more important than wildlife ecology or comparative behavior.

title: Veterinary Technology B.S.
scale: Large public research university · Amherst and Newton, Massachusetts
overview: UMass Amherst offers a four-year B.S. in Veterinary Technology. Students spend the first two years in Amherst and the final two years at the Charles River Campus in Newton for advanced clinical work. The program is accredited by the American Veterinary Medical Association and prepares graduates for the Veterinary Technician National Examination. The published curriculum includes clinical nursing, animal welfare, anatomy and physiology, microbiology, pathology, pharmacology, diagnostic imaging, anesthesia and surgery, laboratory-animal medicine, and senior internships.
fundamental: A four-year, accredited veterinary-technology pathway combining animal science and welfare foundations with progressively advanced clinical nursing and technical training.
scienceFoundation: Biology, chemistry, statistics, anatomy, and physiology
Veterinary microbiology, pathology, pharmacology, and parasitology
Animal welfare and clinical animal behavior or exotic-animal medicine options
Laboratory methods, diagnostic imaging, and evidence-based clinical decision-making
Clinical nursing, anesthesia, surgery, emergency care, and patient monitoring
animalContent: Small- and large-animal clinical nursing
Animal welfare and behavior in clinical care
Diagnostic imaging, clinical laboratory techniques, anesthesia, and surgery
Laboratory-animal medicine and management
Elective exposure to exotic-animal medicine, shelter medicine, emergency care, and conservation/veterinary topics
experience: The first two years include laboratory and animal-science work in Amherst. The final two years move to the dedicated Charles River veterinary-technology facilities in Newton for advanced clinical coursework, community veterinary clinic practica, and senior internships at veterinary clinics or research-animal facilities.
research: The degree explicitly prepares graduates for veterinary medicine and biomedical-research settings. Senior internships can occur in research-animal facilities, and the curriculum includes laboratory-animal medicine; students interested in research should compare available placements and faculty projects when planning the upper-division years.
progression: Years 1–2 in Amherst: biology and chemistry foundations, introductory and large-animal clinical nursing, anatomy and physiology, animal welfare, microbiology, pathology, and behavior/exotics options.
Year 3 in Newton: advanced clinical nursing, pharmacology, clinical laboratory techniques, diagnostic imaging, parasitology, anesthesia, surgery, and community-clinic practice.
Year 4: laboratory-animal medicine, veterinary-medicine problem solving, internships in clinical or research settings, senior seminar, and examination preparation.
Across all four years: build a documented clinical skill set while testing whether companion-animal, emergency, research, exotic, zoo, or another technical setting is the best fit.
resume: B.S. in Veterinary Technology; accredited professional preparation; clinical nursing; anesthesia and surgery; imaging; laboratory methods; animal welfare; patient monitoring; internships; eligibility for the national veterinary-technician examination.
advantages: A direct professional degree rather than a general pre-veterinary pathway.
The curriculum explicitly includes animal welfare and offers behavior/exotic-animal options alongside clinical training.
The Amherst-to-Newton structure places advanced years near Boston-area clinical and research settings.
tradeoffs: The required move from Amherst to Newton after sophomore year is a major structural consideration.
The core curriculum serves veterinary technology broadly; zoo and exotic work would still require deliberate electives, internships, or later specialization.
The program includes large-animal and laboratory-animal material in addition to companion-animal care.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when hands-on animal health care, physiology, technical skill, and patient contact are appealing, but becoming a veterinarian is not assumed to be the goal.

title: Zoology B.S.
scale: Public research university · Durham, New Hampshire
overview: UNH's Zoology B.S. provides in-depth training in animal biology and ecological systems, with laboratory and field experience in physiology, genetics, evolution, and related areas. After a common biology core, students can use upper-level work to concentrate in areas such as behavior, physiology, cell and developmental biology, ecology, evolution, fisheries, neurobiology, or marine and freshwater biology.

Evolution, genetics, ecology, and organismal biology
Physiology, neurobiology, cell biology, and developmental biology options
Laboratory and field research methods
Scientific writing, analysis, and independent research

Behavior and neurobiology options
Physiology and comparative organismal biology

Field- or laboratory-based undergraduate research
experience: UNH emphasizes hands-on learning and direct undergraduate participation in research. Zoology students can pursue field or laboratory projects and have access to biological research facilities across terrestrial, freshwater, estuarine, marine, physiology, aquaculture, and behavioral areas.
research: Research is a defining strength of the degree. The program encourages undergraduates to conduct field- or laboratory-based research and use advanced electives and faculty mentorship to determine later specialization.
progression: Year 1: biology and chemistry foundations plus an introduction to zoology as a discipline.
Year 2: complete core biological and physical-science requirements and begin identifying an animal-biology specialty.
Year 3: choose advanced work in areas such as behavior, physiology, evolution, ecology, development, neurobiology, or fisheries and seek a faculty research experience.
Year 4: deepen the chosen specialty through upper-level electives, independent research, and preparation for employment or graduate study.
resume: B.S. in Zoology; broad animal biology; physiology/genetics/evolution foundation; field and laboratory research; advanced animal-focused electives; potential independent research.
advantages: The degree title and curriculum keep animals central while remaining scientifically broad.
Behavior, physiology, neurobiology, ecology, and other specialties can be explored without changing majors.
Undergraduate research is explicitly encouraged in both laboratory and field settings.
tradeoffs: This is not a professional animal-care or veterinary-technology program.
Direct husbandry, zoo-management, and welfare training are not the organizing core of the major and would need to be added through electives or external experience.
The flexibility of the upper-level curriculum makes careful course selection important.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when animal biology is the intellectual center and behavior or physiology are strong interests, but the student wants to keep several scientific directions open.

title: Zoo Science B.S.
type: Zoo science and managed animal care
overview: Delaware Valley University's Zoo Science B.S. is an unusually direct undergraduate route into zoo and aquarium work. The university states that students work with animals beginning in the first year and study zoo and aquarium management, captive-wildlife conservation, husbandry, handling, nutrition, disease, behavior, training, exhibit design, and small-population management. Required Experience360 work adds internships and other real-world learning.
fundamental: A specialized, hands-on zoo-science degree that integrates husbandry, behavior, health, conservation, and professional zoo/aquarium practice.
scienceFoundation: General biology and organismal science
Ecology, animal behavior, and captive-wildlife conservation
Wildlife nutrition, health, and disease
Animal management and small-population principles
Applied observation, recordkeeping, and professional practice
animalContent: Zoo animal husbandry and handling
Animal training and enrichment
Zoo and aquarium management
Wildlife nutrition, health, disease, mammalogy, ornithology, and herpetology
Exhibit design, record systems, and captive-population management
experience: DelVal says Zoo Science students begin working with animals in the first year. The required Experience360 program includes real-world experience and internships, including animal-care and public-education settings, with access to regional zoo, aquarium, natural-science, and wildlife organizations.
research: Experience360 includes opportunities for student research in addition to internships. Students interested in research-intensive graduate study should compare the exact faculty projects, statistics sequence, and independent-research options available during their enrollment.
progression: Year 1: begin biological science and early animal contact while learning the foundations of zoo science.
Year 2: add behavior, husbandry, handling, nutrition, ecology, and animal-health coursework.
Year 3: deepen zoo and aquarium management, training/enrichment, recordkeeping, and taxon-focused study while building Experience360 placements.
Year 4: complete advanced professional work and substantial internships, using the experience to clarify keeper, behavior, welfare, management, education, or graduate-school goals.
resume: B.S. in Zoo Science; direct animal work; husbandry; behavior and training; enrichment; wildlife nutrition and health; zoo/aquarium management; internships through Experience360.
advantages: The degree directly teaches zoo science rather than requiring students to assemble it from unrelated electives.
Hands-on animal work begins early and continues through required experiential learning.
Behavior, training, enrichment, husbandry, health, and zoo management appear together in one curriculum.
tradeoffs: A specialized zoo-science degree is less broad than a general biology or zoology degree if interests later move away from managed animals.
The wider university has strong agricultural programs, so students should distinguish the Zoo Science curriculum from other animal/agriculture offerings.
Zoo and aquarium careers remain experience-intensive and competitive even with a directly relevant degree.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when zoo/exotic animal care, husbandry, behavior, enrichment, and hands-on experience are already among the strongest interests.

title: Veterinary Technology A.S. / B.S. — Bangor
overview: The University of Maine at Augusta offers both associate and bachelor's degrees in Veterinary Technology at its Bangor campus. UMA describes the program as fully accredited and emphasizes extensive theory, hands-on technical skills, laboratory experience, animal care, and welfare. The associate degree prepares graduates for licensed veterinary-technician work; the bachelor's degree adds depth for areas such as management and research.
fundamental: A Bangor-based veterinary-technology pathway with both associate and bachelor's options and a strong emphasis on practical technical skill and laboratory training.
scienceFoundation: Anatomy, physiology, and animal-health foundations
Clinical laboratory methods and technical procedures
Veterinary nursing and patient-care principles
Animal-care, welfare, and professional practice
Additional upper-level preparation in the bachelor's pathway

Clinical patient care and animal handling
Laboratory procedures and veterinary support

Bachelor's-level extension for management, research, or continued study
experience: UMA emphasizes hands-on technical skills and laboratory experience in onsite Bangor facilities, allowing students to practice procedures in a consistent instructional environment.
research: The bachelor's degree is presented as adding a competitive edge for students interested in veterinary-business management, research, or further education. Prospective students should ask about current faculty projects, external placements, and species-specific opportunities.
progression: Early study: build anatomy, physiology, animal-care, and foundational veterinary-technology skills.
Associate-level progression: develop the technical competencies needed for entry into licensed veterinary-technician practice.
Bachelor's-level progression: add upper-level coursework and broader preparation for management, research, or specialized roles.
Throughout: document hands-on competencies and use clinical experiences to identify preferred species and work settings.
resume: A.S. and/or B.S. in Veterinary Technology; hands-on technical training; laboratory experience; animal care and welfare; professional preparation for veterinary-technician practice.
advantages: Both associate and bachelor's pathways are available within the same Bangor program.
The program explicitly emphasizes hands-on technical training and laboratory experience.
The bachelor's option allows continued study without leaving the veterinary-technology pathway.
tradeoffs: Students should compare the exact associate-versus-bachelor sequence and credentialing milestones before choosing the four-year route.
The public program information emphasizes veterinary technology broadly rather than a dedicated zoo/exotic specialization.
Students interested in zoo or wildlife medicine would still need to seek species-relevant placements and experiences.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when veterinary technology is a serious possibility and a Maine-based, hands-on program with both two- and four-year options is attractive.

title: Veterinary Technology B.S.
scale: Public technology college · Canton, New York
overview: SUNY Canton's Veterinary Technology B.S. builds on and complements its Veterinary Science Technology A.A.S. curriculum. The associate program has been accredited by the American Veterinary Medical Association since 1978, and the B.S. includes the specific coursework required in that associate curriculum plus upper-division science and applied electives. Students work with companion animals, farm animals, and common laboratory animals and can become eligible for the national veterinary-technician examination after meeting the A.A.S. requirements.
fundamental: A four-year veterinary-technology route built on an established accredited associate curriculum, adding advanced technical and upper-division study.
scienceFoundation: Associate-level veterinary science technology core
Anatomy, physiology, clinical laboratory, and animal-health science

Upper-division science and applied electives

experience: The accredited A.A.S. curriculum combines small laboratory sections, extensive hands-on work, kennel-duty rotations, and two clinical preceptorships. The B.S. builds on that foundation with advanced technical and upper-division coursework.
research: The program lists biomedical research, diagnostic laboratories, educational institutions, and zoo/wildlife medicine among potential employment settings. Students interested in research should examine current electives and project opportunities in the bachelor's years.
progression: Years 1–2: complete the veterinary science technology core, hands-on laboratories, animal-care duties, and preceptorship experiences.
Credentialing milestone: once A.A.S. requirements are met, students can become eligible for the national veterinary-technician examination.
Years 3–4: add advanced technical training, upper-division sciences, and applied electives within the B.S.
Use later coursework and placements to test clinical, research, laboratory-animal, zoo/wildlife, supervisory, or other technical directions.
resume: Veterinary Technology B.S. built on an accredited Veterinary Science Technology A.A.S.; companion, farm, and laboratory-animal experience; preceptorships; advanced technical study.
advantages: The B.S. is integrated with a long-established accredited associate veterinary-technology curriculum.
Students gain experience with several animal types rather than only companion animals.
The four-year route allows advanced technical and supervisory preparation while preserving the technician credential pathway.
tradeoffs: The program includes farm and laboratory animals as well as companion species; students seeking only zoo/exotic work should evaluate that species mix carefully.
The A.A.S. is the specifically documented accredited program; the B.S. builds on and includes that curriculum rather than being described here as a separately accredited program.
Zoo/wildlife medicine is a possible work setting, not a dedicated undergraduate specialization.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when a four-year veterinary-technology degree is appealing and broad hands-on exposure across companion, farm, and laboratory animals is acceptable.

title: Veterinary Science Technology A.A.S. → Veterinary Technology B.S.
scale: Public technology college · Delhi, New York
overview: SUNY Delhi offers a two-stage veterinary-technology path: the accredited Veterinary Science Technology A.A.S., followed by a Veterinary Technology B.S. for qualified students who have completed an accredited associate degree and are license-eligible or credentialed. The A.A.S. emphasizes live-animal work from the first semester, anatomy and physiology, anesthesia, surgical and dental assistance, medical care, laboratory work, and experience with companion, farm, and laboratory animals. The B.S. adds advanced veterinary technology, science, management, and focus options in advanced clinical techniques, laboratory-animal science, or public health.
fundamental: An intensive hands-on associate veterinary-technology foundation followed by an optional bachelor's continuation for advanced clinical, laboratory-animal, public-health, or supervisory preparation.

Clinical laboratory, anesthesia, dental, surgical, and medical-care techniques

Advanced science and management in the bachelor's continuation

animalContent: Live-animal laboratories beginning in the first semester

experience: SUNY Delhi emphasizes immediate and repeated live-animal laboratory work. Facilities include surgical and diagnostic-imaging suites, a clinical teaching space, laboratory-animal facilities, and a large-animal teaching farm. The associate program also supports preceptorship and internship-style professional experience.
research: The bachelor's curriculum offers a laboratory-animal science focus, and the wider veterinary-science program prepares students for clinical hospitals and research facilities. Students interested in research should compare the available laboratory-animal electives and external placements.
progression: Years 1–2: complete the accredited A.A.S. with live-animal labs, anatomy and physiology, anesthesia, medical care, imaging, and technical skill development.
Credentialing milestone: A.A.S. graduates are eligible for the national veterinary-technician examination and licensure process.
Years 3–4: qualified students may continue into the B.S. for advanced veterinary technology, science, management, and a selected emphasis.
Use the advanced clinical, laboratory-animal, or public-health options to shape the final years toward the preferred work setting.
resume: Accredited Veterinary Science Technology A.A.S. with optional Veterinary Technology B.S. continuation; extensive live-animal work; anesthesia; surgery support; diagnostic imaging; clinical and laboratory-animal preparation.
advantages: Live-animal experience begins in the first semester and continues throughout the associate program.
The A.A.S. has full American Veterinary Medical Association accreditation, with a clear credentialing route before bachelor's completion.
The B.S. adds advanced focus choices rather than simply repeating entry-level technician training.
tradeoffs: Admission to the B.S. requires an accredited veterinary-technology associate degree plus academic and license-eligibility requirements; it is not simply four undifferentiated years from freshman entry.
The program's animal mix includes farm and laboratory animals, so students should be comfortable with a broad veterinary curriculum.
Zoo/exotic medicine is not the organizing emphasis of the degree and would need to be pursued through placements or later specialization.
bestWhen: Especially relevant when very early hands-on veterinary training is appealing and the student likes the option to earn the technician credential after an associate degree before continuing into advanced bachelor's work.
